description: Only claims backed by a fetched public source are listed. Secondary sources are explicitly marked; unverified search summaries remain excluded.

claims.text: Google Arts & Culture derives rangoli from Sanskrit rangavalli and translates it as rows of colours.
The Asian Art Museum translates Deepavali as a row of lights.
Google Arts & Culture describes rangoli as made during Diwali and other festivals, in homes, courtyards, and sometimes on walls.
The cited museum resources describe women making rangoli and passing designs across generations.
Google Arts & Culture lists rice powder, brick powder, chalk powder, flower petals, and coloured sand among rangoli materials.
The Asian Art Museum describes the belief that rangoli invites divine blessings and says some designs invite Lakshmi at the threshold; attribute this as a belief, not a universal fact.
claims.usage_note: Always phrase as belief attributed to the source.

claims.text: Google Arts & Culture describes kolam as symmetric lines and loops around a dot grid, with festive designs larger and more elaborate.
The Asian Art Museum lists regional threshold-art names including kolam, muggu, rangoli, chowk purana, mandana, alpana, chita, and aipan.
The Asian Art Museum describes rangoli as temporary and reflects on its disappearance remaining in the maker's memory.
claims.usage_note: Paraphrased; do not use a longer quotation without attribution and review.

claims.text: Wikipedia's secondary overview describes chowk purana as beginning with a square, then adding circles or triangles inside.
Asia InCH describes Sohrai as a post-harvest festival observed the day after Diwali and identifies domestic wall murals as its primary visual expression.
claims.usage_note: Attribute this as one documented account; dates and local practice can vary.

public_copy.text: In some communities, homes are illuminated and rangoli is made at doorways for Diwali.
